segments.en: Friday night in Oistins. Fish sizzles on open grills, music thumps from the speakers, and older couples dance beside families sharing plates of grilled marlin and macaroni pie. This is a fine place to meet Barbados.

Barbados is a small coral island, sitting a little apart from the rest of the Caribbean chain, out in the Atlantic. Its people call themselves Bajans, and they are famously warm and quick with a joke.
Listen closely and you will hear Bajan dialect, a musical, rolling way of speaking English. A friend might greet you with wuh happenin, and you can simply answer, all good.
The national dish is cou-cou and flying fish. Cou-cou is a smooth mix of cornmeal and okra, and the flying fish, which really do glide above the waves, is steamed in a spicy sauce.
Bridgetown, the capital, has a busy harbour, colourful shopfronts and a historic district that is protected as world heritage. Nearby, the old Garrison Savannah hosts horse racing on sunny weekends.

Look out for chattel houses, small wooden homes painted pink, blue and yellow. They were built on blocks, not foundations, so that workers who did not own land could take their homes apart and move them.
For centuries, sugar cane covered the island, and from it came rum. Many villages still have a small rum shop where neighbours meet to chat and slap down dominoes.
When the sugar harvest ends, the island celebrates Crop Over. For weeks there are calypso contests and street parties, ending with Grand Kadooment, a parade of dazzling costumes dancing to soca.
Cricket here is a way of life. Barbados has produced some of the greatest players ever to hold a bat, including Sir Garfield Sobers, and every village seems to have a pitch.
The west coast is calm, with gentle turquoise water and soft sand. On the wild east coast, at Bathsheba, huge Atlantic waves crash around giant boulders, and surfers ride the swell.
Beneath the island, Harrison's Cave glitters with stalactites and clear streams. And in the forests, you might spot green monkeys leaping through the branches.
Good manners matter. Say good morning when you enter a shop or climb onto a bus, and Sunday is often for church in your best clothes, followed by a big family lunch.
When you are ready to move on, sail west toward the Caribbean Sea, where Saint Lucia is waiting with its green twin peaks rising from the water.
